1: This briefing is Book 10 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Cloud Boundary and Landing Zone.
Its argument is simple: the authorization boundary, not the product catalog, decides which cloud features an agency can actually use.
We'll take four questions in turn.
Why does the boundary decide what you can use?
And how do you get there?
If you remember one thing, make it this: treat the boundary as a list you can read, not a perimeter you can only accept, and evidence every choice in your own package.
The slides and notes carry every detail and citation; I'll stick to what matters.
Let's start with why the boundary decides.
2: Here's why the boundary matters, in one example.
Two agencies hold the same Microsoft 365 license.
One runs a commercial tenant and gets network assessments, smarter routing and Adoption Score.
The other runs G C C and gets none of them, because Microsoft documents each one as unavailable there.
That happens because three parties make three separate decisions.
fed-ramp certifies a specific offering, and the Marketplace is the record.
The provider publishes, feature by feature, what each government environment leaves out.
And the agency authorizes its own system, with its authorizing official accepting the risk of what it configures and connects.
What you can use is where all three overlap.
So a feature with no citation isn't available.
Next, why that gap stays hidden for so long.
3: So why don't people see the gap sooner?
Because it's invisible until a design depends on it.
The surfaces are shared: Intune in G C C is the same instance as commercial Intune.
The exclusions are scattered, one sentence per feature page.
A detection whose input never arrives looks exactly like a quiet day.

The book then tests a widely repeated example, that five features are silently missing from G C C. Checked against Microsoft's documentation, only one is: the Locations view of network connectivity in the admin center.
The others turn out to be G C C High and DoD gaps, not documented gaps at all, or inside Azure's own scope.
The lesson: an unverified boundary story sends an agency off to build compensations it doesn't need.
Now, what actually changes across a boundary.
4: To reason about any boundary, the book uses its own model.
A boundary is any surface across which four things change.
Telemetry: which signals actually arrive on your side.
Identity: who a claim's issuer resolves to, and G C C pairs with Entra ID in commercial Azure, while G C C High and DoD pair with Azure Government.
Enforcement: who has to enforce a control, which in G C C often means the agency's own measurements.
And provenance: whether a claim is still authoritative, or only derived.
Each of these raises its own kind of drift, and detection for them is at different stages; the slide shows where each stands.
One more point worth holding onto.
fed-ramp's definition of federal customer data excludes the telemetry a provider generates.
No certification promises you a signal.
5: fed-ramp itself changed in 2026, and three changes matter here.

First, services are now certified in classes, A through D. Class C covers today's Moderate baseline and Class D today's High, and agencies can still authorize at whatever security category they judge appropriate.
Second, the new rules have no provider authorization boundary at all.
The phrase doesn't appear once in the machine-readable ruleset, and security category may vary by resource.
Third, change is notified rather than re-approved, and the deadlines are counted in business days.
Routine changes need no notice; bigger ones have set notice windows, and the slide lists them.
Two dates are worth writing down: adoption is mandatory on January 1, 2027, and new Rev5 requests stop on June 11, 2027.
Now let's read what G C C actually is.
6: Chapter 04 reads G C C from Microsoft's own documents.
G C C is the worldwide service, minus a published list of exclusions.
And that list isn't a ladder.
Some features, like network connectivity in the admin center and Adoption Score, are missing in G C C, G C C High and DoD alike.
Others reach G C C and stop there.
The biggest documented loss is the network connectivity layer: a daily score for each location, with performance attributed to named network providers.
A G C C agency has to fund its own measurement instead.
On the Marketplace, the G C C package is certified at Class C, Moderate, and a second package with the same name is in process at Class D.
But G C C High is already Class D, and it still lacks network connectivity.
A higher class doesn't bring back an excluded feature.
7: The landing zone is where the boundary stops being a diagram and becomes policy.
Each workload gets a subscription, placed in a management group that carries its rules.
The baseline hierarchy puts an intermediate root under the tenant root, and that's where boundary policy lives.
Platform groups hold shared services like security and connectivity; landing zone groups hold the workloads.
Make Sandbox the default, so no new subscription lands outside the boundary policy.
Each boundary decision then gets a mechanism, from allowed locations and resource types to exemptions that carry an expiry date; the slide maps them.
Roll every policy out in audit mode first.
One catch: Microsoft's accelerators are supported only in public Azure, so in Azure Government the platform team adapts the code by hand.
8: Chapter 06 makes the address plan the join key for the evidence.
A scan tells you what answered; the eye-pam tells you what was allocated.
So every inventory reconciles against it, and BOD 23-01 already asks for automated discovery every seven days.
In Azure, the enterprise eye-pam stays the authority.
Reserve the block there first, mirror it into Virtual Network Manager pools, then use policy to deny any virtual network without an allocation, and reconcile by discovery.
Virtual Network Manager isn't named in Microsoft's fed-ramp audit scope, so record it as a dependency until coverage is confirmed.
The book builds all this as layered modules, each writing its state as evidence.
And it treats outside inputs as code too, like the monthly Microsoft endpoint list a G C C tenant uses.
9: Code anyone can apply from a laptop isn't change control.
So Chapter 07 adds a front door: a governed request into the landing zone, which Microsoft calls subscription vending.
The loop runs from request, through approval, plan, apply and reconcile, to close.
The requester can't approve their own request, and the approver reviews the actual plan before anything changes.
The reconcile step carries the most weight.
The pipeline writes the address allocation back to the enterprise eye-pam, and fails the run if the two disagree, because an unreconciled block is shadow inventory the moment it exists.
The pipeline sits inside the boundary question too.
Terraform state is sensitive data, and not every pipeline service is on the Marketplace.
So the default is a self-hosted runner, with state kept inside the agency's boundary.
10: The rule is one decider per row.
The authorizing official determines the boundary, signs every exception, and decides whether a change needs reauthorization.
That risk acceptance can't be delegated, and in federal agencies it's held by government personnel only.
The system owner is the boundary owner.
They keep the boundary record and the package, and they decide where a new workload goes.
That matters, because vending an unrecorded subscription is the cheapest way to turn an authorized system into an unauthorized one.
The see-so sets control requirements, and the I S S O reads provider change notices against the record.
The platform team builds everything, but doesn't decide whether a gap is acceptable.
And the contract is a boundary decision too: only a contracting officer changes what the agency bought.
11: So what do you do with a capability that's outside the boundary?
nist gives four options: compensate, accept more risk, choose a more trustworthy provider, or don't use the service.
The work starts with a register, one feature per row, each tied to the provider's own statement.
Only vendor-confirmed rows support a claim to a provider or an assessor.
Then probe what actually works in your tenant, on a schedule, testing for the output rather than the switch.
Where a gap is real, build an in-boundary equivalent and say it's derived.
Or take an exception, where the authorizing official signs a dated risk acceptance.
And one practical warning: buy the capability, not the badge.
Microsoft's Network Provider Program, for example, is closed to new providers.
12: The third answer is an alternative path: move the workload to a different certified service, and leave the identity plane where it is.
Google Workspace and Gemini for Government are separate listings at different classes, so which AI features sit inside which certification is a question for the package.
The public record shows both outcomes.
One cabinet-level department moved more than 50,000 employees to Google Workspace in 2025.
A military department went the other way, ending about 150,000 Google email licenses after an audit found few in use.
Whichever way you go, keep Entra ID as the source.
Provision users, federate sign-in and apply Conditional Access there.
Then close the gaps: Google super administrators sign in outside it, and Google's directory is derived, so report drift.
13: Finally, the boundary has to show up in the agency's own package.
The agency never authorizes a cloud service; it authorizes its own system that uses one.
So its plan should hold only what the agency is responsible for, and fed-ramp is blunt: don't copy and paste provider controls into it.

Instead, write the boundary down once, as a record the system owner keeps, and cite it everywhere: the system description, each external service, each crossing, the POA&M and the component definitions.
Know whose package you're reading, too.
G C C runs on Azure Government, so the inheritance chain runs through two provider packages.
And a compensating narrative takes just four sentences: what the control needs, what's unavailable, what runs instead, and where the remaining gap is recorded.
Next, what to ask your provider for.
14: Appendix A turns all of this into requests to the provider.
Three habits make a request hard to deflect: name one item, cite the basis with a link, and ask for data, not documents.
The book makes eight requests, and the slide lists them.
One number shows why trust centers made the list: when the book checked, only 110 of 781 Marketplace listings had a trust-center entry, and none of the Microsoft 365 government packages did.
Five of the eight requests rest on obligations the rules already place on providers.
And if the answer is no, a documented no is evidence too.
15: Build the feature register on cited rows only, and drop or relabel anything without a vendor page.
Name the boundary owner: the authorizing official decides the boundary, and the system owner keeps the record and gates every new subscription.
Enforce the boundary in the landing zone, with policy at the intermediate root, audit before deny, and the governed front door.
And evidence every response, whether it's an equivalent, an exception or an alternative path, in the agency's own package.
Before your next architecture review, list every cloud feature your designs depend on, with its package, its availability in your environment, and the page that says so.
Then put Appendix A's requests to your provider.
The license says what you bought; the boundary says what you may use.
Book 10 has the detail, every claim footnoted.
